Coefficient H (Maximal Reliability) With a Confidence Interval

Source: R/reliability_H.R
reliability_H.Rd

Estimates coefficient H (Hancock & Mueller, 2001), the reliability of the optimally weighted composite of the items that measure one factor, and returns a confidence interval for the population coefficient. H is the largest reliability that any weighted sum of the items can reach under the factor model, whereas McDonald's \(\omega\) (reliability_omega) is the reliability of the unit-weighted sum that people usually score. The coefficient can be computed from a fitted lavaan model (fit, the recommended input), from raw item scores (data), from a covariance matrix and its sample size (S and N), or from the standardized loadings a paper reports (loadings). The interval comes from the delta method with the full covariance matrix of the parameter estimates, built on the logit scale by default, or from a nonparametric bootstrap when one is requested.

Usage

reliability_H(
  loadings = NULL,
  se_loadings = NULL,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  fit = NULL,
  factor = NULL,
  group = NULL,
  data = NULL,
  S = NULL,
  N = NULL,
  vcov_loadings = NULL,
  ci_method = c("mlr_logistic", "mlr", "ml_logistic", "ml", "delta_logistic", "delta",
    "bootstrap_se", "bootstrap_se_logistic", "percentile", "bca", "none"),
  missing = c("fiml", "listwise"),
  aux = NULL,
  B = 10000,
  seed = NULL,
  ncpus = 1L,
  progress = NULL
)

Arguments

loadings

Numeric vector of the standardized loadings of one factor, each in \((-1, 1)\), at least two. A fitted lavaan model supplied in this position is taken as fit, so reliability_H(fit) works.

se_loadings

Optional vector of the marginal standard errors of the standardized loadings, the same length as loadings. The interval it gives ignores the covariances among the loading estimates and warns that it does; prefer vcov_loadings or fit.

conf_level

Confidence level for the interval. Defaults to 0.95.

fit

A fitted lavaan model (from lavaan::cfa(), lavaan::sem(), or fa_confirmatory(output = "fit")), the recommended input; see Details.

factor

With fit, the name of the factor whose H is wanted; required when the model has more than one factor measured by observed items.

group

With a multiple group fit, the label of the group (as lavaan::lavInspect(fit, "group.label") gives it) whose H is wanted; required for such a fit.

data

A numeric matrix or data frame of item scores of one scale (rows are respondents, columns are items, three or more), and, when aux is supplied, the auxiliary columns. An item column that is not numeric (or logical), and an item that takes a single value in the rows analyzed, are refused by name before any fit, as is a zero variance on the diagonal of S: the single-factor model cannot be fit with such an item (lavaan would stop on it with an error that names no variable). SPSS user-defined missing values, which haven::read_sav(user_na = TRUE) keeps as values of a haven_labelled_spss column, are missing, as SPSS treats them.

S

A symmetric covariance matrix among the items (three or more); N is then required, and only "ml_logistic", "ml", and "none" apply.

N

Sample size. Required with S; optional with loadings, where it is recorded in the table; not used with fit or data, which count their own cases.

vcov_loadings

With loadings, the \(J \times J\) covariance matrix of the standardized loading estimates, for the delta method interval with the full covariance matrix.

ci_method

Method for the confidence interval. "delta_logistic" and "delta" use the delta method with the covariance matrix that comes with the input (the fit's, or vcov_loadings); "mlr_logistic", "mlr", "ml_logistic", and "ml" name the standard error of the single-factor model fitted to data or S (robust maximum likelihood or maximum likelihood); "percentile", "bca", "bootstrap_se", and "bootstrap_se_logistic" are nonparametric bootstraps (with data, or with a single-group fit that carries its raw data); "none" returns the point estimate. The _logistic methods build the interval on the logit scale. When not supplied, the default is "mlr_logistic" with data, "ml_logistic" with S, and "delta_logistic" with fit and with loadings that come with vcov_loadings or se_loadings; for loadings without either it is "none", since nothing is then known about their sampling variability. A method that does not apply to the input stops with a message naming the ones that do.

missing

With data, how incomplete rows are handled: "fiml" (the default; full information maximum likelihood) or "listwise". The default analysis is FIML whenever an item value is missing and the complete data analysis otherwise (data in which no value is missing, or none but in rows with every item missing, which both treatments drop, are fitted as they stand), as in reliability_omega and unlike fa_confirmatory; see Details. Under listwise deletion the single-factor model needs more complete rows than items (with no more, their covariance matrix is singular and the maximum likelihood fit is not defined), and the function stops before the fit when there are not. Ordinary FIML instead evaluates the constrained measurement model. A failure of the unrestricted H1 diagnostic does not alone invalidate its proper identified estimate or H0-based uncertainty; the result carries an explicit qualification. Supplied two-stage fits require valid unrestricted first-stage moments even for a point estimate. See cov_fiml for the sufficient affine-collapse diagnostic and its limits. Bootstrap resamples retain the family's separate distinct-case screen.

aux

With data, an optional character vector naming auxiliary variable columns of data, entered as saturated correlates under full information maximum likelihood; supplying it implies missing = "fiml".

B

Number of bootstrap replications when a bootstrap method is selected, a single whole number. Defaults to 10000, the reliability family's default; every replication refits a model (see Details for the cost). The fewest accepted depends on the interval method and the level: at the default conf_level, 400 for "percentile" (10 replications beyond each limit), 2000 for "bca" (50 beyond each nominal limit, because the adjusted limits sit farther into the tails), and 100 for "bootstrap_se" and "bootstrap_se_logistic" (a standard deviation of the replications); at 0.99 the first two are 2000 and 10000. A smaller B is refused before anything is computed (class dmar_count_invalid). The count is held to the number requested. Replications set aside afterward are counted and reported in a warning of class dmar_bootstrap_replications_dropped, which names the function and says to request more when those that return a value are fewer than the number required; when fewer than half of the B replications return a value, the interval is withheld (limits and bootstrap standard error NA) under a warning of class dmar_bootstrap_insufficient. See dmar_bootstrap, which also describes options(dmar.bootstrap_exploratory = TRUE) for a first look with a smaller B.

seed

Random number seed for the bootstrap. Defaults to NULL, under which the resamples are drawn from, and advance, the current random number stream; a supplied seed is set for the call, and the caller's RNG state is restored when it returns.

ncpus

The number of processes over which the bootstrap replications are spread. The default 1 runs them in this R session; a larger number uses forked workers (boot's parallel = "multicore") or, on Windows, which cannot fork, a socket cluster ("snow"), whose workers load the installed DMAR. boot draws every resample before any replication runs, so a given seed returns the same interval, counts, and replicates whatever ncpus is. A session that forks workers and also starts background processes through callr or processx needs the environment variable PROCESSX_NOTIFY_OLD_SIGCHLD set before processx is loaded (see sem_exact_fit_bootstrap). A replication whose solution is improper is always set aside, since H is not defined for it. Ignored unless a bootstrap method is selected.

Bootstrap intervals from supplied two-stage fits currently refuse separately stored auxiliary variables: each refit must resample and carry those values with the items. Use an eligible delta interval where available, or explicitly resample and refit them together.

progress

NULL (the default), or a function of two arguments that the bootstrap calls as it runs, so that an application can show how far a long bootstrap has gone and let its user stop it (a Shiny app, for example). It is called as progress(done, total), with the number of replications attempted so far and B: after each replication when ncpus = 1, and with more processes after each block of replications they complete together, about a fiftieth of B (ncpus * ceiling(B / (50 * ncpus)) replications, the last block possibly fewer), so that done advances by the block. A BCa interval takes its acceleration from a regression on the resampling frequencies when at least as many replications return a value as there are cases, and from the jackknife, one leave-one-out refit per case, when fewer do or when that regression fails or gives influence values that are not all finite; the jackknife runs at most once in a call, and not at all when no interval is formed or every returned replicate has the same value. While it runs, the callback is called again after each refit (with more processes, after each block of ncpus * ceiling(n / (50 * ncpus)) refits, n the number of cases resampled), with done and total both B, so it can be called more than B times, and done equal to total does not mean that the bootstrap has finished. If the callback returns FALSE, the bootstrap stops before the next replication or block with an error of class dmar_bootstrap_cancelled, whose elements done and total say how far it got (see dmar_metadata); any other value is ignored. An error inside the callback stops the call with an error of class dmar_progress_error, whose message names the callback and which carries done, total, and, as parent, the callback's own condition with its class intact, so that an application can tell a failing callback from a failing analysis. The callback runs outside the random number stream, so a given seed returns the same result with or without it, and a callback that draws random numbers leaves the caller's stream as it found it. With NULL nothing is called. Ignored unless a bootstrap method is selected.

Value

The reliability family's table (class c("dmar_reliability", "dmar_tbl", "data.frame")), with columns term and value and rows "estimate" (H), "se" (its standard error: delta method, or the standard deviation of the bootstrap replicates; NA for ci_method = "none"), "ci_lower" and "ci_upper", "conf_level", "N" (the cases the fit used, in the named group of a multiple group fit; NA for loadings without N), "N_complete" (the cases complete on the factor's items), and "n_items" (the number of items). Attributes record the computation: coefficient ("H"), ci_method (the method used), missing ("listwise", "fiml", the fit's own label such as "pairwise", or "unknown" for loadings), vcov_basis ("full" when the delta method used the full covariance matrix of the estimates, "diagonal" when only marginal standard errors were supplied, "none" when no delta method standard error was formed), se_type (the lavaan standard error type of the fit; NA for loadings), factor and group (with fit; NA otherwise), metric ("observed", "latent_response" for ordered items, or "unknown" for loadings), residual_covariances (the number of residual covariances inside the block that entered the weights), and loadings (the standardized loadings of the block, named by item). With loadings, vcov_supplied records what came with them, whether or not an interval was formed: "full" for vcov_loadings, "diagonal" for se_loadings, and "none" for neither, in which case the printed table says what an interval would need. With data, aux is recorded when supplied. A bootstrap call also records B and the family's bootstrap attribute (the replications attempted, returned, and set aside, with the reasons; see reliability_omega), which here also carries bias, the mean of the returned replicates minus the estimate (NA when no interval is formed). Its no_solution counts the resamples of three items whose correlations admit no single-factor solution, which are among the improper ones (on the data path; zero with fit, whose refits are not checked for it), and improper_kept is zero, since H is not defined for an improper solution.

Details

The coefficient. For a factor \(f\) measured by items \(b\) that load on it alone, with unstandardized loadings \(\lambda\), residual covariance matrix \(\Theta_{bb}\), and model implied factor variance \(\phi_f\), $$q = \phi_f \, \lambda' \Theta_{bb}^{-1} \lambda, \qquad H = \frac{q}{1 + q}.$$ With uncorrelated residuals and standardized loadings \(\ell_j\) this is the form Hancock and Mueller (2001) gave, $$H = \frac{\sum_j \ell_j^2 / (1 - \ell_j^2)} {1 + \sum_j \ell_j^2 / (1 - \ell_j^2)},$$ in which each item contributes its ratio of common to unique variance, \(\ell_j^2 / (1 - \ell_j^2)\). The weights that reach H are proportional to \(\Theta_{bb}^{-1} \lambda\), so an item counts in proportion to its loading divided by its residual variance, and adding an item can never lower H. Gabler and Raykov (2017, Eq. 9) showed that the same expression with a nondiagonal \(\Theta_{bb}\) is the maximal reliability when residuals inside the block are correlated; a fitted model with residual covariances among the factor's items gets that coefficient here, and the printed table says how many entered the weights. Rescaling the factor rescales \(\lambda\) and \(\phi_f\) inversely, so H does not depend on whether the factor was identified by a marker item or by fixing its variance.

Two further readings of the number are useful. H is the squared correlation between the factor and its best linear predictor from the block's items, the regression factor score computed from those items alone, so it is the reliability of that score: for a one-factor model the determinacy that factor_scores reports is the square root of H. And because H is the largest reliability any weighting of the items can reach under the fitted model, it is at least the model implied \(\omega\) of the unit-weighted sum from the same fit (Raykov, 1997), with equality when the weights \(\Theta_{bb}^{-1} \lambda\) are all equal, which with uncorrelated residuals means equal standardized loadings. Robust omega, whose denominator is the observed variance of the composite, need not lie below it.

Reading H with care. The sample H is a positively biased estimator of the population coefficient, and a composite formed with weights estimated from the sample is on average less reliable than the population H. Aguirre-Urreta, Rönkkö, and McIntosh (2019) found both effects pronounced in small samples (around N = 100), diminishing as the sample grows and barely noticeable beyond about 1,000, although with three items of modest loadings even 1,000 cases left more than 1% bias; the reliability estimate of the unit-weighted composite was nearly unbiased in the same conditions. Report \(\omega\), with its interval, for a scale that people will score by summing or averaging its items, and H as the ceiling that optimal weights could reach, or as the reliability of scores computed from the factor model. A bootstrap call estimates the bias of the sample H (the bias element of the bootstrap attribute), and the printed table shows it.

The four inputs. Exactly one of fit, data, S, and loadings is supplied.

fit

A fitted lavaan model, from lavaan::cfa(), lavaan::sem(), or fa_confirmatory(output = "fit"); the recommended input, because it carries everything the coefficient and its interval need, and the model can be the one the analysis reports. Any factor measured by observed items can be named with factor (a factor of a confirmatory model, or an exogenous or endogenous factor of a structural model), and any group of a multiple group model with group. H is read from the fitted matrices, and its standard error comes from the fit's own covariance matrix of the estimates, so it is the standard, robust, or FIML standard error the model was fitted with. With ordered items fitted by WLSMV (either parameterization) H is the maximal reliability of the latent responses behind the categories, not of the observed categories; the metric attribute and the printed table say so. A loading or a regression the model holds at zero is not one, whether it is fixed (0*item) or constrained (a*item with a == 0, directly or through a chain of equality constraints between labels, as in a == b with b == 0): the model written with that term is the model written without it and gets the same H, so an item listed under the factor with its loading held at zero is not one of the factor's items, and a cross-loading held at zero refuses nothing. A fit is refused, with a message naming the remedy, when an item of the factor also loads on another factor or is regressed on another variable (for the factors of a bifactor model, bifactor_indices reports the index that Rodriguez, Reise, and Haviland, 2016, call H, which counts the other factors' common variance as uncorrelated error and is not this maximal reliability, and, in its "maximal_reliability" attribute, the maximal reliability the fitted model implies for each factor, and ci_bifactor_indices gives both a confidence interval), when the factor is measured by other factors, when an observed covariate predicts the factor, when the solution is improper (an item's residual variance that is not positive, for which H is not defined), and when a factor or a group must be named and is not.

data

Raw scores on the items of one scale. The single-factor congeneric model is fitted exactly as reliability_omega fits it, so H and \(\omega\) rest on the same fit, the same cases, and the same kind of standard error, and missing and aux work as they do there. Three or more items are required, since the model is not identified with two.

S

A covariance matrix among the items, with its sample size N; the same single-factor model, fitted by maximum likelihood.

loadings

The standardized loadings of one factor, as a paper reports them, with the closed form above (which assumes uncorrelated residuals). For an interval, supply vcov_loadings, the covariance matrix of the standardized loading estimates (for example the matching block of lavaan::lavInspect(fit, "vcov.std.all")); se_loadings, their marginal standard errors, is accepted, but it ignores the covariances and warns that it does. Loadings alone carry nothing an interval can be formed from, so without either the estimate is returned with se and the limits NA, and the printed table says what an interval would need.

The interval. The delta method variance of \(\hat H\) is \(g' V g\), where \(V\) is the covariance matrix of all the free parameter estimates of the fit and \(g\) is the gradient of H with respect to them, computed by central differences of the closed form above. \(V\) is used only when it can be, by the check the factor analysis tables (fa_confirmatory, fa_bifactor, fa_second_order) make before they report a standard error: when lavaan could not compute it, or computed it from an information matrix, observed or expected, that is singular in the directions the fit's equality constraints leave free (scaled to a unit diagonal, its smallest eigenvalue is below \(10^{-6}\)), a parameter of the fit is not identified at the estimates and \(g' V g\) means nothing. The estimate is then returned with se and the limits NA, and with the warning, of class dmar_result_qualified, that those tables give for the same fit: the same words for a singular matrix, and for one lavaan could not compute a sentence that ends by naming the standard error and interval of H rather than the tables' columns. The check is of the whole fit, as the tables make it, so a factor whose own parameters are identified loses its interval beside one whose parameters are not. An interval from se_loadings uses only the marginal standard errors of the standardized loadings, the diagonal of \(V\). The loading estimates of a fitted factor model are correlated, and the diagonal can understate or overstate the variance: in seven blocks of three to six tests from holzinger_swineford, each fitted as one factor, the standard error from the full matrix ranged from about 0.7 to 1.3 times the one from the diagonal. By default the Wald interval is built on the logit scale and transformed back (Browne, 1982): the limits of a monotone transformation of a parameter are the transformation of its limits, the confidence interval transformation principle that Kelley (2007) sets out, so the interval stays inside (0, 1) and is asymmetric near the upper bound, as the sampling distribution of a high reliability is; "delta", "ml", and "mlr" give the untransformed Wald interval. The default standard error depends on the input: with data, the robust maximum likelihood standard error (Satorra-Bentler, or Yuan-Bentler under FIML), as for \(\omega\), because Kelley and Pornprasertmanit (2016) found the normal theory Wald interval wanting when items depart from normality; with S, the maximum likelihood standard error; and with fit, the fit's own. With fit, "ml" and "mlr" (and their _logistic forms) are accepted when they name the standard error the fit already carries, and otherwise stop with a message saying which one it carries.

The delta method interval is the fast default. For a reported analysis, the percentile or BCa bootstrap with the model refitted on every replication (by FIML when data are missing) is the safer choice, as it is for \(\omega\) (Kelley & Pornprasertmanit, 2016), and it also estimates the bias of the sample H. With data the rows are resampled and the single-factor model refitted; with fit the rows the model was fitted to are resampled and the model itself refitted through lavaan::lavaan(), with the fitted estimates as starting values (for a single-group fit that carries its raw data). Before any resample is drawn, the model is refitted this way to the rows of fit itself, and the call stops unless that refit reproduces the estimate, so the replications are refits of the model the estimate describes. A fit with sampling weights is refused, since a resample of its rows does not carry them and every replication would be an unweighted fit, and so is a fit with a cluster variable, whose cases are not independent and cannot be resampled one at a time; the delta method interval, built from the fit's own covariance matrix of the estimates, serves both. The bootstrap engine is the one the whole reliability family uses (Efron & Tibshirani, 1993): replications that fail to converge, give an improper solution (or, with three items, a resample whose correlations admit no single-factor solution), or raise an error are set aside and counted (a resample in which an item takes a single value is refused before the refit, by name, as the data would be; lavaan would stop on the item after printing its table of the variables; so is a resample with too few distinct cases, by the rule of missing with data, and with fit by the rule of the fit's own treatment of incomplete rows: under listwise deletion, or with complete data, one with no more distinct rows than the model's continuous variables, whose sample covariance matrix is singular, and under FIML or two-stage estimation one with no more distinct cases that observe a variable, while a fit by pairwise deletion is held to neither), and the counts travel in the bootstrap attribute, print under the table, and are stated in a warning. A replication whose likelihood has no maximum (an error variance running off below zero while the likelihood is flat or still rising; see fa_bifactor) is counted among those that raised an error, and a fit with no maximum behind the estimate itself stops with an error of class dmar_no_maximum, which with data prints the lavaan code of the single-factor fit, where bounds = "pos.var" or a different model are the choices. H is not defined for an improper solution, so the attribute records improper_rule = "drop". Each replication is a model fit, a few hundredths of a second for a one-factor model on complete data and longer under FIML, so the default B = 10000 (the family's default, chosen for the stability of the BCa quantiles) takes minutes. The examples therefore stop at the delta method; the bootstrap call for their five verbal tests is reliability_H(data = holzinger_swineford[, verbal], ci_method = "bca", B = 2000, seed = 113).

Missing data. With data, incomplete items are fitted by default by full information maximum likelihood (FIML), which keeps every case with at least one observed item or observed auxiliary variable, with auxiliary variables (aux) entered as saturated correlates (Graham, 2003), and missing = "listwise" fits the complete rows alone; data in which no value is missing, and S, are fitted as they stand. A row with every item missing does not count as incomplete data, since without auxiliary variables both treatments drop it. The default analysis is therefore FIML whenever an item value is missing and the complete data analysis otherwise, unlike fa_confirmatory, which fits complete data by FIML too. That is the rule of reliability_omega, whose complete-data intervals need the complete data analysis, and it is followed here so that the two fit the same single-factor model the same way; on incomplete data it agrees with fa_confirmatory. With fit, the fit's own treatment applies: a model fitted with missing = "ml" gives H and its standard error by FIML. Either way N counts the cases the fit used and N_complete those complete on the factor's items, so the cost of listwise deletion is visible. Under missing = "fiml" a pair of items or auxiliary variables that no case observes together is refused by name before any fit, since the data carry no information about its covariance (lavaan only warns, and its EM returns an arbitrary value for it), and so is a pair the cases observe together only where one of them takes a single value, since those cases carry none about how the two vary together; in a bootstrap, a resample that leaves such a pair is set aside with the same message and counted.

From standardized loadings. With loadings alone the function returns the estimate, with se and the limits NA, because standardized loadings carry nothing an interval can be formed from (the default ci_method is then "none"). With vcov_loadings the interval is the delta method interval from the full covariance matrix of the loading estimates. With se_loadings it is the delta method interval from their marginal standard errors, and the call warns every time, with class dmar_H_marginal_se, that the interval ignores the covariances among the loading estimates. Every input returns the reliability family table described under Value; the sampling variance of H is the square of the row se. reliability(type = "H") dispatches here.

The coefficient that fa_confirmatory reports as H_<factor> is the same quantity, with lavaan's delta method standard error and an untransformed interval; reliability_H(fit, factor = "speed", ci_method = "delta") reproduces its estimate and standard error for the factor speed.

References

Aguirre-Urreta, M. I., Rönkkö, M., & McIntosh, C. N. (2019). A cautionary note on the finite sample behavior of maximal reliability. Psychological Methods, 24(2), 236–252. doi:10.1037/met0000176

Browne, M. W. (1982). Covariance structures. In D. M. Hawkins (Ed.), Topics in applied multivariate analysis (pp. 72–141). Cambridge, UK: Cambridge University Press.

Efron, B., & Tibshirani, R. J. (1993). An introduction to the bootstrap. New York, NY: Chapman & Hall/CRC.

Gabler, S., & Raykov, T. (2017). Evaluation of maximal reliability for unidimensional measuring instruments with correlated errors. Structural Equation Modeling, 24(1), 104–111. doi:10.1080/10705511.2016.1159916

Graham, J. W. (2003). Adding missing-data-relevant variables to FIML-based structural equation models. Structural Equation Modeling, 10(1), 80–100. doi:10.1207/S15328007SEM1001_4

Hancock, G. R., & Mueller, R. O. (2001). Rethinking construct reliability within latent variable systems. In R. Cudeck, S. du Toit, & D. Sörbom (Eds.), Structural equation modeling: Present and future (pp. 195–216). Scientific Software International.

Kelley, K. (2007). Confidence intervals for standardized effect sizes: Theory, application, and implementation. Journal of Statistical Software, 20(8), 1–24. doi:10.18637/jss.v020.i08

Kelley, K., & Pornprasertmanit, S. (2016). Confidence intervals for population reliability coefficients: Evaluation of methods, recommendations, and software for composite measures. Psychological Methods, 21, 69–92. doi:10.1037/a0040086

Raykov, T. (1997). Estimation of composite reliability for congeneric measures. Applied Psychological Measurement, 21(2), 173–184. doi:10.1177/01466216970212006

Rodriguez, A., Reise, S. P., & Haviland, M. G. (2016). Evaluating bifactor models: Calculating and interpreting statistical indices. Psychological Methods, 21(2), 137–150. doi:10.1037/met0000045

See also

reliability_omega for the reliability of the unit-weighted composite, reliability for the family's general entry point, factor_scores for the scores whose reliability H is, fa_confirmatory for the fit, and bifactor_indices for the bifactor index of Rodriguez, Reise, and Haviland (2016) and the maximal reliability of each factor of a bifactor model.

Other reliability: cohen_kappa(), diagnosis_agreement, fleiss_kappa(), icc(), reliability(), reliability_alpha(), reliability_kr20(), reliability_omega(), reliability_omega_categorical()

Author

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu

Examples

verbal <- c("t5_general_information", "t6_paragraph_comprehension",
            "t7_sentence", "t8_word_classification", "t9_word_meaning")

# From raw item scores: the single-factor model is fitted here, and the
# interval uses its robust maximum likelihood standard error on the
# logit scale.
reliability_H(data = holzinger_swineford[, verbal])
#>  term       value
#>  estimate   0.918
#>  se         0.007
#>  ci_lower   0.903
#>  ci_upper   0.931
#>  conf_level 0.950
#>  N          301  
#>  N_complete 301  
#>  n_items    5    

# The omega of the unit-weighted sum from the same model, for
# comparison; H is the ceiling that optimal weights could reach.
reliability_omega(data = holzinger_swineford[, verbal],
                  denominator = "model_implied")
#>  term       value
#>  estimate   0.902
#>  se         0.010
#>  ci_lower   0.881
#>  ci_upper   0.919
#>  conf_level 0.950
#>  N          301  
#>  N_complete 301  
#>  n_items    5    
#> 
#> Denominator: composite variance implied by the fitted model
#> Largest residual correlation under the single-factor model: -0.040 (t8_word_classification with t9_word_meaning)

# From a fitted model with several factors, name the factor. The
# standard error is the fit's own, from the full covariance matrix of
# its estimates (requires lavaan).
fit <- lavaan::cfa(
  "visual  =~ t1_visual_perception + t2_cubes + t4_lozenges
   textual =~ t6_paragraph_comprehension + t7_sentence + t9_word_meaning
   speed   =~ t10_addition + t12_counting_groups_of_dots +
              t13_straight_and_curved_capitals",
  data = holzinger_swineford, std.lv = TRUE)
h <- reliability_H(fit, factor = "textual")
h
#>  term       value
#>  estimate   0.885
#>  se         0.011
#>  ci_lower   0.861
#>  ci_upper   0.906
#>  conf_level 0.950
#>  N          301  
#>  N_complete 301  
#>  n_items    3    
#> 
#> Factor: textual
attr(h, "loadings")
#> t6_paragraph_comprehension                t7_sentence 
#>                  0.8515822                  0.8550655 
#>            t9_word_meaning 
#>                  0.8380103 

# From the standardized loadings a paper reports, without an interval.
reliability_H(loadings = c(0.6, 0.7, 0.8), ci_method = "none")
#>  term       value
#>  estimate   0.767
#>  se         <NA>

#>  ci_upper   <NA> 
#>  conf_level 0.950
#>  N          <NA> 
#>  N_complete <NA> 
#>  n_items    3    
#> 
#> No interval (ci_method = "none"): an interval from standardized loadings needs 'vcov_loadings', the covariance matrix of their estimates

generics::tidy(h)
